strengths: Clear identification and systematic study of an important practical problem (sequential unlearning requests) that existing literature overlooks
Strong empirical diagnosis of root cause: cumulative parameter drift is well-demonstrated through Figure 4 and validated theoretically via Taylor expansion analysis
Well-designed evaluation framework using standardized UnlearnCanvas benchmark with objective metrics (UA, RA-I, RA-C) rather than relying on subjective evaluation
Comprehensive exploration of multiple regularization approaches (L1/L2, SelFT, Model Merging, Gradient Projection) with clear motivation and complementarity analysis
Novel insight connecting semantic similarity to retention difficulty via cross-attention projection matrices, with strong empirical correlation (r = -0.627)
Practical design philosophy emphasizing add-on mechanisms compatible with existing unlearning methods (ConAbl, EraseDiff), increasing real-world applicability
Rigorous experimental methodology with systematic evaluation across multiple unlearning requests, clear visualization of utility collapse, and thorough ablation studies
Solid theoretical grounding with formal bounds and first-order invariance guarantee (Lemma 7.1) for the proposed gradient projection method
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of individual components: L1/L2 regularization is standard, Selective Fine-tuning builds on Fan et al. (2023), Model Merging uses existing TIES-Merging, and gradient projection is established in continual learning; contribution is primarily in combination rather than novel algorithms

Narrow evaluation scope: only 12 sequential requests tested (unclear if scales to 50+), limited to 80 concepts from UnlearnCanvas, no evaluation on out-of-distribution concepts or human perceptual studies
Substantial remaining performance gaps: in-domain retention is only ~30-40% even after applying all proposed methods (Figure 6), raising questions about practical utility

Critical implementation details missing or vague: auxiliary concept generation via LLM is underspecified (which LLM? prompting strategy? number of candidates?), hyperparameter sensitivity analysis absent (λ for regularization, k% for SelFT, M for gradient projection)

Incomplete theoretical analysis: Taylor bound is standard and loose; explains that drift matters but not why sequential application fundamentally accumulates drift differently; no characterization of fundamental limits or necessary conditions for continual unlearning

Gradient projection method shows trade-offs: slightly worse cross-domain retention (RA-C) than alternatives in object unlearning, only provides first-order invariance (higher-order effects may still accumulate), requires additional LLM-based preprocessing
Limited baseline comparisons: no adaptation of established continual learning methods (EWC, A-GEM, DER), no experience replay approach, limited exploration of alternative merging strategies

Significant methodological gaps: Figure 7a shows correlation for only one target concept (should validate across multiple), no study of how unlearning order affects drift, no computational cost analysis, reproducibility concerns regarding LLM-based auxiliary concept generation

strengths: Identifies an important and practical problem (continual unlearning) that is largely unexplored in image generation, with clear motivation through compelling visual examples
Provides systematic diagnosis of the root cause—cumulative parameter drift—supported by both empirical observation (Figure 4) and theoretical analysis (Taylor expansion bound)

Insightful empirical finding that retention difficulty correlates strongly with text-embedding similarity to unlearned concepts (Figure 7a, r=-0.627), suggesting semantic-aware regularization is needed
Proposes practical, add-on compatible solutions that work across different unlearning methods (ConAbl, EraseDiff), increasing adoptability

Well-structured presentation with clear progression from problem identification to diagnosis to solutions; informative figures and metrics (UA, RA-I, RA-C distinguish in-domain vs. cross-domain retention)
Multiple complementary approaches at different complexity levels (simple L1/L2 regularization to semantic-aware gradient projection) that can be combined for further gains
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: L1/L2 regularization, selective fine-tuning, and model merging are borrowed from existing continual learning/unlearning work without substantial modification; gradient projection, while contextually novel, is a straightforward orthogonal projection technique

Critical evaluation gap: In-domain retention (RA-I) remains severely degraded (30-40% after 6-9 requests) despite all proposed solutions, suggesting the methods fundamentally fail to solve the stated problem

Narrow evaluation scope: Only one model (Stable Diffusion v2), one dataset (UNLEARNCANVAS with 80 concepts), relatively short sequences (12 requests), and template-based prompts—generalizability to other models, domains, and realistic use cases (person removal, copyrighted content) is unclear

Gradient projection method is underspecified: Auxiliary concept generation via LLM is vague (how many M? sensitive to choice?), the text-embedding space may not be the right proxy for diffusion model subspace interference, and first-order invariance (Lemma 7.1) provides no second-order guarantees

Missing critical evaluations: No human evaluation of image quality/concept removal (relies entirely on CLIP-based classifiers), no failure case analysis, no statistical significance testing, limited error bars suggesting insufficient random seeds, no comparison to rehearsal-based continual learning baselines

Weak ablation studies: Missing analysis of hyperparameter sensitivity (how to choose λ, k%, M?), no comparison to continual learning methods (EWC, SI, A-GEM), no exploration of request order sensitivity, limited investigation of why in-domain retention is so difficult

Theoretical analysis limitations: Taylor expansion bound is loose and doesn't explain when retention succeeds; does not explain why simultaneous strategy has less drift than sequential; limited engagement with continual learning theory on catastrophic forgetting

Limited scale: Only 12-request sequences tested; real-world systems might need to handle 100s of requests. Unclear if findings scale with sequence length or to more realistic concept types (person identities, artistic styles beyond UNLEARNCANVAS, harmful content)

Methodological concerns: Evaluation assumes CLIP-based classifiers are robust and OOD-reliable; assumes unlearning targets known a priori (impractical); cross-attention analysis assumes single-token concepts; no evaluation of computational costs or application to parameter-efficient methods like LoRA

strengths: First systematic study of continual unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models, addressing a practical gap where requests arrive sequentially rather than in batch
Clear root cause diagnosis: cumulative parameter drift from pre-training weights, backed by empirical analysis (Figure 4) and theoretical motivation (Taylor expansion)
Multiple compatible regularization solutions (L1/L2, SelFT, Model Merge) designed for practical integration with existing methods, demonstrating broader applicability
Novel gradient projection method motivated by strong empirical correlation (r=-0.627) between text-embedding similarity and retention difficulty, with principled mathematical formulation
Rigorous experimental methodology using UnlearnCanvas benchmark with consistent evaluation protocol (UA, RA-I, RA-C) across two domains and two baseline methods
Well-organized presentation with effective visualizations clearly demonstrating the problem and solution effectiveness
Thorough ablations and compatibility analysis showing that methods complement each other and benefits grow with sequence length
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: L1/L2 regularization, selective fine-tuning, and model merging are standard techniques adapted from continual learning; gradient projection is straightforward subspace projection
In-domain retention problem remains substantially unsolved: RA-I drops to 20-30% after 12 requests despite all proposed methods, with persistent gap vs. RA-C (Figures 6, 9)

Theoretical analysis is loose and provides limited mechanistic insight: Taylor expansion bound doesn't predict which regularizers work better, and doesn't explain the superiority of gradient projection

Gradient projection method underspecified: auxiliary concept selection procedure vague ('filtered by text-embedding similarity'), sensitivity to M unexplored, applicability when auxiliary concepts unavailable unclear
Limited experimental scope: single model architecture (Stable Diffusion v2), only 60 styles + 20 objects, maximum 12 sequential requests, no evaluation on other popular models

Missing implementation details and hyperparameter guidance: λ selection process not documented, no sensitivity analysis, computational cost not discussed, reproducibility concerns (code not mentioned as available)

Incomplete design space exploration: no comparison with non-regularization approaches (replay-based, architecture-based methods), missing ablations on auxiliary concept count M for gradient projection
Theoretical-practical gap: the analysis motivating regularization doesn't explain why gradient projection specifically works, limiting understanding of when/why different solutions are preferable

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: sequential unlearning is more realistic than simultaneous requests
Comprehensive empirical study across multiple methods, domains, architectures, and metrics with extensive supplementary experiments
Clear diagnostic analysis of root causes through parameter drift analysis (both empirical and theoretical)
Proposed solutions are pragmatic and plug-and-play, compatible with existing unlearning methods
Well-written paper with clear presentation and informative visualizations
Good insight about semantic similarity as predictor of in-domain retention degradation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: L1/L2 regularization and selective fine-tuning are standard; model merging directly applies existing TIES-Merging; only gradient projection is novel but relatively straightforward
Weak theoretical foundation for gradient projection: Lemma 7.1 is trivial, no convergence guarantees, first-order approximation insufficient for higher-order parameter interactions
Gradient projection method underspecified: number of auxiliary concepts M not justified, no sensitivity analysis, no discussion of LLM failure modes or concept selection criteria
Persistent fundamental challenge inadequately addressed: even best method shows large RA-I vs RA-C gap, especially for object unlearning, suggesting limitations not fully resolved
Evaluation limitations: classifier-based metrics may not capture all degradation modes, no human evaluation, narrow comparison scope (limited LLM baselines), missing ablations on key hyperparameters

Incomplete analysis of core phenomena: why sequential exhibits more drift despite fewer steps unexplored; all-or-nothing erasure behavior noted but underdeveloped; results inconsistent across architectures (model merge outperforms gradient projection on SDXL)
Narrow experimental scope: only 60 styles + 20 objects, limited architecture coverage, specialized fine-tuned classifiers for evaluation, no analysis of longer sequences (>12 concepts)
Reproducibility concerns: no code provided, gradient projection implementation details sparse, hyperparameters (k for SelFT) not clearly reported, computational cost comparison insufficient
Theoretical contributions limited: Taylor expansion bound is standard from continual learning; analysis largely confirms intuitions without deep insights specific to diffusion models or unlearning

Practical limitations underexplored: model merging requires training |C| independent models (computational cost), auxiliary concept acquisition and robustness not addressed, generalization to other unlearning types unclear

strengths: Novel and practical problem formulation: First systematic study of continual unlearning in text-to-image generation, addressing realistic sequential request scenarios

Clear problem demonstration and diagnosis: Excellent empirical evidence of utility collapse with compelling visualizations; root cause (cumulative parameter drift) convincingly identified through parameter norm analysis

Thorough and comprehensive evaluation: Multiple metrics (UA, RA-I, RA-C) distinguishing in-domain vs. cross-domain retention; validated across style, object, and celebrity unlearning; tested on multiple architectures (Stable Diffusion, SDXL) and methods (ConAbl, SculpMem, ESD)

Strong empirical analysis: Taylor expansion analysis (Section 5.2) with supporting Hessian estimation; Appendix D convincingly shows drift is intrinsic to sequential unlearning via controlled early-stopping experiments

Semantic-aware gradient projection: Well-motivated method with strong empirical correlation (r=-0.627) between text-embedding similarity and retention difficulty; principled approach grounded in cross-attention mechanism; demonstrates complementarity with other regularizers
Practical applicability: Suite of add-on regularizers can integrate with existing methods; provides practitioners with multiple options (L1/L2, SelFT, model merge, gradient projection)

Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Clear writing, effective visualizations, thorough appendix with extensive additional results and analyses; uses established benchmark (UnlearnCanvas); promises code release
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Individual techniques largely apply existing methods (L1/L2 regularization, Selective Fine-Tuning adapts Nguyen et al. 2024, Model Merge uses TIES-Merging, gradient projection uses standard orthogonal projection). While the application is novel, the core algorithmic contributions are incremental

Incomplete mechanistic understanding of sequential drift: Paper identifies that sequential unlearning accumulates drift but does not fully explain why this happens fundamentally. Section 8 provides observations (anchor-based learning, all-or-nothing erasure) but lacks deep theoretical grounding. The gap between showing that drift happens and understanding why sequential causes more drift than simultaneous persists

Gradient projection method limitations: (1) Auxiliary concept selection via LLM + cosine similarity filtering is ad-hoc with no sensitivity analysis; (2) Number of auxiliary concepts M not studied; (3) Only applies to cross-attention (WK, WV), leaving other interference mechanisms unexplored; (4) Guarantees first-order invariance (Lemma 7.1) but ignores higher-order effects; (5) Underperforms model merge on SDXL+ESD (Figure 16-17) without clear explanation

Limited evaluation scope: Sequence length only 12 concepts (6 for celebrities)—behavior at much longer sequences unclear; primarily Stable Diffusion/SDXL; CLIP-based evaluation may not capture all quality degradation; no systematic evaluation across random seeds

Missing practical guidance: No systematic hyperparameter selection guidance (λ, k%, M); computational cost of gradient projection not analyzed; handling of adversarially ordered requests not discussed; unclear when to prefer model merge vs. gradient projection

Incomplete robustness analysis: No evaluation of adversarial recovery attacks on unlearned concepts; all-or-nothing erasure pattern (Appendix C) is concerning but not analyzed for robustness to perturbations; security implications of sharp transitions not addressed
Persisting in-domain retention gap: RA-I remains substantially lower than RA-C even with gradient projection (Figure 6), suggesting the fundamental problem is only partially solved

Underexplored model merge: Performs best overall but receives limited analysis; computational cost of independent unlearnings not discussed; all-or-nothing erasure complicates interpolation without proposed solutions
